video.title: Why You Get Tight, and How to Fix It | Learning From Sinner's 6-0 6-1 Masterclass

classification.reason: The coach analyzes Jannik Sinner's forehand mechanics from match footage to explain why players get tight and how to build upstream mechanics to trust the swing.

problem.title_as_question: Why do you get tight and hesitate on your forehand, and how can you fix it to swing in a flow state?
problem.definition: Players lose trust, get tight, and hesitate during their forehand because they attempt to micromanage racket angles and contact instead of relying on upstream body levers and footwork probing to release the arm naturally.

symptoms.description: Hesitation, lack of confidence, and feeling terrified that the racket face is too open or too closed through contact.
Tightening up the arm and pushing or slicing the ball across instead of completing a free forward release.
Errant ball flight sailing long or catching the net caused by conscious micro-manipulation of the racket angle.
Stroke timing and execution breakdown when trying to rocket the ball with excessive shoulder effort.

causes.statement: The forward flick and roll through contact occurs in under half a second, making it far too rapid for verbal cues or conscious racket-angle manipulation.
The player lacks trust in the release because they have not identified a single comfortable arm sensation and built upstream trunk and non-dominant arm mechanics around it.
The player fails to establish the precise comfortable strike distance relative to the body through intentional foot-eye probing, forcing the body to tighten up and compensate.
The player attempts to generate shot velocity by overhitting directly with the shoulder rather than through positive balance and trunk twisting coordination.

angles.summary: The forward forearm-shoulder roll and flick occurs in under half a second, making conscious kinesthetic corrections impossible during contact.
Players only get one single atomic sensation through contact, such as feeling how the hand comes through or throwing the shoulder back.
Jannik Sinner uses his left arm leverage and wide stance to aim and propel his hitting arm without active manipulation at contact.
Trusting the forehand is not a mental problem; it requires practicing the natural arm release repeatedly and coordinating upstream body levers around it.
Foot-eye probing to locate the exact comfortable strike zone resembles the coordinated footwork of playing soccer.

solutions.summary: Focus on a single atomic sensation through contact, such as how the hand comes through or feeling the shoulder, rather than thinking about verbal mechanical cues.
Use your trunk angle and left shoulder leverage to aim and fire the right arm through, trusting the hitting arm to release without manipulation.
Stay low in an athletic double-bend stance and connect your feet directly to your eyes to intentionally probe and establish your comfortable strike position.
Check that your back foot finishes forward of where it prepped, verifying that positive weight transfer drives the shot rather than shoulder overhitting.
solutions.external_goal: Check that the back foot finishes a foot in front of the baseline

solutions.summary: Perform medicine ball throws to groove the neuromuscular pattern of coordinating trunk twisting with forward weight transfer.
solutions.external_goal: Throw a heavy medicine ball while coordinating weight transfer and trunk twist
